The jailer wakes and, thinking the prisoners have escaped, is about to kill himself, but Paul shouts that they are all there. Trembling, the jailer asks what he must do to be saved, and they answer: believe in the Lord Jesus, and you and your household will be saved. He washes their wounds, and he and his household are baptized that night and rejoice.
pages.look_closer: Their feet are in stocks and their backs are bleeding, yet at midnight they pray and sing, and the other prisoners listen (verses 24-25). When the doors open, none escape, and the jailer hears the good news instead of fleeing (verses 27-31).
lessons: Praise does not wait for good circumstances. Paul and Silas sing in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25).
God can use a prison for good. The jailer and his household come to faith (Acts 16:29-34).
The way of salvation is plain: believe in the Lord Jesus (Acts 16:30-31).
Faith and good order go together. Paul asks that the officials come themselves and respect their rights as citizens (Acts 16:35-39).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand how a household comes to faith and is baptized, and how spirits are driven out, in different ways. This page says only what the text says.

pages.title: Rahab and the Spies of Jericho
pages.summary: Joshua secretly sends two men from Shittim to spy out the land, especially Jericho, and they stay at the house of a prostitute named Rahab. The king of Jericho hears of it and orders Rahab to hand the men over, but she hides them under stalks of flax on her roof and tells the king's men that they left at dusk, sending them in the wrong direction. Rahab tells the spies she knows the LORD has given them the land, that everyone is afraid of them because of what he did at the Red Sea, and that the LORD rules over heaven and earth. She asks them to promise to spare her family, and they agree. She lowers them by a rope through the window of her house on the city wall, and they tell her to tie a scarlet cord in the window and keep her family inside. The spies return to Joshua and say that the LORD has surely given them the land.
pages.look_closer: Rahab has heard what the LORD did at the Red Sea, and she acts on what she heard (verses 9-11). The hiding place is a roof with flax, and the sign of safety is a red cord in a window (verses 6, 18). The New Testament remembers her faith (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25).
lessons: Faith can start with a story. Rahab hears what God has done and believes (Joshua 2:9-11).
Faith acts. She risks her life to protect God's people (Joshua 2:4-6, 15).
God's mercy reaches unlikely people. He saves Rahab and her family (Joshua 2:12-14; 6:25).
She is remembered in the line of Jesus and in the list of the faithful (Matthew 1:5; Hebrews 11:31).

pages.title: Samson and Delilah
pages.summary: Samson, whom the LORD has made very strong, falls in love with a woman named Delilah, and the Philistine rulers each offer her eleven hundred pieces of silver to find out the secret of his strength. Three times she asks him, and three times he gives a false answer, and each time she tests it while he sleeps and calls out that the Philistines are upon him. Day after day she nags him until he gives in and tells her that no razor has ever touched his head, because he has been a Nazirite to God since birth. She has his hair cut while he sleeps, and the Philistines seize him, put out his eyes and make him grind grain in prison. His hair begins to grow again. At a great festival for their god Dagon, they bring him out to entertain them, and he prays that the LORD will remember him and give him strength once more. He pushes against the two central pillars, and the temple falls.
pages.look_closer: The secret is not the hair itself but Samson's vow to God, of which the hair is a sign (verse 17). When the hair goes, he does not know that the LORD has left him (verse 20). His last prayer comes only after the hair has begun to grow again (verses 22, 28).
lessons: Strength is a gift with a purpose. Samson's strength comes from God and is tied to his vow (Judges 16:17).
Small compromises add up. Samson plays with the secret three times before he gives it away (Judges 16:6-17).
Losing God's presence can happen without noticing. Samson does not know the LORD has left him (Judges 16:20).
God still hears a broken man's prayer. Samson cries out and is answered (Judges 16:28-30).

pages.title: Solomon Asks for Wisdom
pages.summary: Solomon loves the LORD and goes to Gibeon to offer sacrifices, and there at night the LORD appears to him in a dream and says, Ask what I should give you. Solomon thanks God for his faithfulness to David, says he is only a young man who does not know how to lead, and asks for an understanding heart to govern the people and tell right from wrong. God is pleased that he did not ask for a long life, riches or the death of his enemies, and promises him a wise and discerning heart like no one before or after, as well as the riches and honor he did not ask for. Soon afterward two women come to Solomon, each claiming that a baby is hers. He calls for a sword to cut the living child in two, and the true mother cries out to give the baby to the other woman. Solomon knows she is the mother, and all Israel marvels at his wisdom.
pages.look_closer: Solomon does not ask for riches or a long life, and God gives him wisdom and also what he did not ask for (verses 11-13). The wisdom is tested at once, with a real child and real mothers (verses 16-27).
lessons: Humility is the beginning of wisdom. Solomon knows he is young and needs help to lead (1 Kings 3:7-9).
Ask God for what you need to do the work he has given you, not only for what you want for yourself (1 Kings 3:9-11).
God gives more than we ask when our hearts are in the right place (1 Kings 3:12-13).
Wisdom shows in how we judge. Solomon finds the true mother by a test that reveals love (1 Kings 3:24-28).

pages.title: The Boy Jesus in the Temple
also: Jesus in the temple as a boy
pages.summary: Every year Mary and Joseph go to Jerusalem for the Passover feast. When Jesus is twelve, the family goes up as usual, but on the way home the boy stays behind in Jerusalem and his parents do not realize it. Thinking he is somewhere in the group, they travel a whole day before they start looking for him among relatives and friends. When they cannot find him, they go back to Jerusalem and search for three days. At last they spot him in the temple, seated with the teachers, listening to them and asking questions, and everyone who hears him is amazed at his understanding. Mary says they have been anxious, and Jesus asks why they were looking, since he had to be in his Father's house. They do not understand, but he goes home with them to Nazareth and obeys them.
pages.look_closer: Jesus calls the temple his Father's house, just after Mary has said 'your father and I' (verses 48-49). Luke then says he went home and obeyed them (verse 51). He is both the Son of God and a child who submits to his parents.
lessons: Jesus knows from a young age who his Father is and what he is here for (Luke 2:49).
Even the Son of God listens, learns and asks questions. Wisdom grows with time and attention (Luke 2:46, 52).
He obeys his parents though he knows his true Father. Obedience at home is part of growing up in wisdom (Luke 2:51-52).
Parents can lose track of a child, and God can use even that to show something. Mary keeps these things in her heart (Luke 2:48, 51).

pages.title: The Crucifixion of Jesus
pages.summary: Roman soldiers take Jesus into the governor's headquarters, dress him in a purple robe, press a crown of thorns on his head and mock him as King of the Jews. Then they lead him out to be crucified, later a passer-by named Simon, from Cyrene, is forced to carry the cross the rest of the way. At the place called Golgotha, Jesus is crucified between two robbers, with a sign above Him that reads: The King of the Jews. People passing by, the chief priests and even one of the men crucified beside him ridicule Him. At midday darkness covers the whole land for three hours. Then Jesus cries out in a loud voice and breathes his last. The curtain of the temple is torn in two, from the top down, and the centurion who watched him die says that this man truly was the Son of God. Women who had followed him from Galilee watch from a distance.
pages.look_closer: Watch who speaks. Soldiers, passers-by and priests all say he should save himself (verses 29-32), yet the first to name him is a Roman officer who sees how he dies (verse 39). The torn curtain (verse 38) is explained later: the way into God's presence is open, restored access (Hebrews 10:19-20).
lessons: Jesus is mocked as a king and dies under a sign that calls him King of the Jews. People meant it as an insult; it is exactly who He is (Mark 15:17-18, 26).
He does not come down from the cross when they dare him to. Staying there is the way He saves everyone (Mark 15:30-32).
The Roman officer who watches him die is the first to say who He is. Faith can begin at the foot of the cross, even for an outsider (Mark 15:39).
Scripture says our forgiveness was bought at a great price: not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18-19).

passages.label: Insults, darkness and his last cry

pages.title: The Fiery Furnace
also: the three friends in the fire
the fourth man in the furnace
pages.summary: King Nebuchadnezzar sets up a golden statue ninety feet high and orders everyone to bow down to it when the music plays, or be thrown into a blazing furnace. Some astrologers report that three Jews, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, whom the king had put in charge of the province, do not bow. The furious king gives them one more chance, but they answer that their God is able to rescue them, and even if he does not, they will not serve his gods or worship the statue. The king orders the furnace heated seven times hotter and has them bound and thrown in, and the heat kills the soldiers who carry them. Then Nebuchadnezzar leaps up in amazement: he sees four men walking about in the fire, unbound and unharmed, and the fourth one looks like a divine being. He calls them out, and they have no burns, and not even the smell of smoke. The king praises their God and decrees respect for him.
pages.look_closer: The three do not say that God will rescue them. They say he is able to, 'but even if he does not' they will not bow (verses 17-18). Their faithfulness does not depend on the outcome.
lessons: Some things we will not bow to. The three friends choose God even when the penalty is fire (Daniel 3:16-18).
Faith trusts God's power without demanding a particular result: 'but even if he does not' (Daniel 3:17-18).
God meets us in the fire. A fourth figure walks with the three in the furnace (Daniel 3:24-25).
Faithful witness can change what a king says. Nebuchadnezzar praises their God (Daniel 3:28-29).

passages.label: A fourth man in the fire

pages.title: The First Passover
pages.summary: God tells Moses and Aaron that this month will be the first month of the year. On the tenth day each family is to take a lamb without defect, keep it until the fourteenth day, and kill it at twilight. They are to smear some of its blood on the doorposts and the beam above the door of the house where they eat it, and eat the roasted meat that night with bitter herbs and bread made without yeast, dressed to travel and in haste. That night the LORD will pass through Egypt and strike every firstborn, but where he sees the blood he will pass over that house. The day is to be remembered every year as a feast. Moses tells the elders, and the people bow down and do as they are told. At midnight the LORD strikes every firstborn in Egypt, there is loud crying, and Pharaoh tells the Israelites to go. They leave in haste, carrying dough before it has risen.
pages.look_closer: The blood on the doorframe is a sign for the LORD (verse 13), and the meal is eaten ready to leave: cloak tucked in, sandals on, staff in hand (verse 11). Rescue and departure belong together.
lessons: God provides a way of rescue. The blood of the lamb marks the house (Exodus 12:7, 13).
Trust shows in obedience. Each family does just as God said (Exodus 12:28).
Rescue means leaving. They eat ready to go (Exodus 12:11, 31-34).
The Passover is to be remembered, and for Christians it points to Christ, our Passover lamb (Exodus 12:14; 1 Corinthians 5:7).

pages.title: The Golden Calf
pages.summary: While Moses is on the mountain for a long time, the people gather around Aaron and tell him to make gods for them, since they do not know what has happened to Moses. Aaron collects their gold earrings and shapes a molten calf, and the people say it is the god who brought them out of Egypt. Aaron builds an altar and announces a feast, and the next day they sacrifice, then sit down to eat and drink and play. The LORD tells Moses the people have quickly turned aside and offers to make a great nation of Moses instead. Moses pleads for them and reminds God of his promises to Abraham, Isaac and Israel, and God relents. Moses comes down with the stone tablets, and when he sees the calf and the dancing he throws them down and breaks them. He burns the calf and grinds it to powder. Later he goes back to the LORD and asks him to forgive their sin.
pages.look_closer: The LORD speaks of 'your people, whom you brought up' and Moses answers 'Your people, whom You brought out' (verses 7, 11). Each hands the people back to the other. Moses stands in the gap and even offers to be blotted out for them (verse 32).
lessons: Impatience can turn into idolatry. When Moses seems delayed, the people make a god they can see (Exodus 32:1-4).
Leaders can fail under pressure. Aaron gives in and builds the altar (Exodus 32:2-5, 21-24).
Intercession matters. Moses pleads for the people, and God relents from the disaster (Exodus 32:11-14).
Sin is serious, and forgiveness is costly. Moses goes back to ask the LORD to forgive, even offering himself (Exodus 32:30-32).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand what it means to be blotted out of God's book in different ways, and how God's anger and God's mercy relate. This page says only what the text says: God relents, Moses asks for forgiveness, and the people still face the result of what they did.

pages.title: The Handwriting on the Wall
pages.summary: King Belshazzar gives a great feast for a thousand nobles and, while drinking wine, orders that the gold and silver cups taken from God's temple in Jerusalem be brought in, so that they can drink from them and praise their gods. Suddenly the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plaster of the palace wall. The king turns pale and his knees shake, and none of his wise men can read or explain the writing. The queen remembers Daniel, and he is brought in. He refuses the rewards offered, reminds the king how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar for his pride, and says Belshazzar has not humbled himself but has lifted himself up against the Lord. Daniel reads the words and explains that God has numbered the days of his kingdom, weighed him and found him lacking, and given his kingdom to the Medes and Persians. That same night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede takes the kingdom.
pages.look_closer: Belshazzar knew how God had humbled Nebuchadnezzar, and still he did not humble his heart (verses 18-22). The writing is brief: numbered, weighed, divided (verses 25-28).
lessons: God notices how we treat what is holy. Belshazzar's drinking from the temple cups is an insult to him (Daniel 5:2-4, 23).
Pride ignores history. Belshazzar knows how God humbled Nebuchadnezzar and does not learn from it (Daniel 5:20-22).
God's servants speak the truth without fear or reward. Daniel refuses the gifts and tells the king what the writing means (Daniel 5:17, 25-28).
God's judgment comes at the time he has set. That very night the kingdom changes hands (Daniel 5:26-31).

pages.title: The Last Supper
pages.summary: It is the day of Unleavened Bread, and Jesus sends Peter and John to get the Passover meal ready. He tells them a man with a water jar will lead them to a large furnished upper room, and they find everything just as he said. That evening Jesus sits at the table with his apostles and says how much he has longed to eat this Passover with them before he suffers. He gives thanks over a cup and over the bread, breaks the bread and gives it to them, saying it is his body given for them and that they should do this to remember him. After supper he takes the cup and calls it the new covenant in his blood, poured out for them. Then he says that the one who will betray him is at the table, and the apostles begin asking one another who it could be.
pages.look_closer: Notice how much Jesus says before the bread and cup are passed round. He has longed for this meal, and he speaks of the kingdom of God (verses 15-18). The Supper is set inside Passover, the feast of rescue, and looks ahead to the day he drinks with them again.
lessons: Jesus knows what lies ahead and still prepares a meal for his friends, even though one of them will betray him (Luke 22:8-13, 21-22).
He gives the bread and the cup a meaning: his body given and his blood poured out for them. Everything he is about to suffer is for others (Luke 22:19-20).
He asks his followers to keep doing this to remember him, so the meal looks back to the cross and forward to the kingdom (Luke 22:16-20).
Even among the twelve the question of who will fail is real, and they begin to ask it of themselves. The meal invites honest hearts (Luke 22:21-23).

passages.label: One of you will betray me

pages.doctrine_note: Christians keep this meal with different names (the Lord's Supper, Communion, the Eucharist) and understand the bread and the cup in different ways, including who may share it and what happens in it. This page says only what the text says: what Jesus did, what he said, and that he asked his followers to remember him.

pages.title: The Lost Sheep and the Lost Coin
also: the parable of the lost sheep
pages.summary: Tax collectors and sinners are gathering around Jesus to listen, while the Pharisees and the experts in the law complain that he welcomes sinners and eats with them. So Jesus tells them a parable. A man who has a hundred sheep and loses one leaves the ninety-nine in the open country and goes after the lost one until he finds it. He puts it on his shoulders, full of joy, goes home and calls his friends and neighbors to celebrate. Jesus says heaven celebrates one repenting sinner more than ninety-nine righteous people who feel no need to repent. Then he tells of a woman with ten silver coins who loses one. She lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches carefully until she finds it, and calls her friends to rejoice with her. In the same way, Jesus says, God's angels rejoice over one sinner who repents.
pages.look_closer: Both parables end the same way: the lost thing is found, friends are called, and there is joy (verses 5-6, 9). The Pharisees grumbled about who Jesus eats with (verse 2). The answer is that heaven celebrates when one lost person comes home.
lessons: God goes looking. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to find one (Luke 15:4).
Every person matters. One sheep out of a hundred, one coin out of ten (Luke 15:4, 8).
Finding the lost brings joy, and God shares it with his friends and angels (Luke 15:6-7, 9-10).
Jesus eats with sinners because that is what the Good Shepherd does (Luke 15:1-2).

pages.title: The Parable of the Talents
pages.summary: Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a man going on a journey who calls his servants and entrusts his property to them. He gives five talents to one, two to another and one to a third, each according to his ability, and then leaves. The servant with five goes at once and trades with them and gains five more, and the one with two gains two more. The one who received one digs a hole in the ground and hides his master's money. Much later the master returns and settles accounts. The first two each report their gains, and the master says: well done, good and faithful servant; come and share your master's joy. The third says he was afraid, knew his master was a hard man, and hid the money, and he gives it back. The master calls him wicked and lazy, takes the talent from him and gives it to the one with ten.
pages.look_closer: The first two servants do the same thing with different amounts, and they receive the same praise (verses 21, 23). The third does nothing and blames his fear of the master (verses 24-25). The story is about what we do with what we have been given while the master is away.
lessons: Everything we have is entrusted to us, and the master expects it to be used (Matthew 25:14-15).
Faithfulness is measured by effort, not size. The two-talent servant gets the same words of praise (Matthew 25:21-23).
Fear can bury our gifts. The third servant hides his talent (Matthew 25:25).
There will be an accounting, and the Lord's joy is the reward for faithful servants (Matthew 25:19-23).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand the final judgment pictured in this parable, including what happens to the third servant, in different ways. This page says only what the text says.

pages.title: The Ten Commandments at Sinai
pages.summary: Three months after leaving Egypt, the Israelites camp at Mount Sinai, and God speaks all these words to them. He begins by reminding them that he brought them out of slavery. The first commands are about God: no other gods, no carved images, do not misuse the LORD's name, and keep the Sabbath day holy by resting, as he rested after creating. The rest are about people: honor your father and mother, no murder, no adultery, no stealing, no lying against a neighbor, and no coveting what belongs to someone else. When the people see the thunder, lightning, trumpet sound and smoke on the mountain, they tremble and stand far off. They ask Moses to speak to them instead, afraid that God's voice will kill them, and Moses answers that God has come to test them so that they will fear him and not sin.
pages.look_closer: The commandments begin with rescue, not rules: God first reminds them that he brought them out of slavery (verse 2). The first four are about God and the last six about people (verses 3-17). The people respond with fear (verses 18-21).
lessons: God gives his law to people he has already rescued. Rescue comes first, then the way to live (Exodus 20:1-2).
The first commands are about loving God alone, without rivals or images (Exodus 20:3-6).
The others protect people: family, life, marriage, property, truth and the heart (Exodus 20:12-17).
The Sabbath is a gift of rest and remembering (Exodus 20:8-11).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians number the commandments in different ways, and understand the Sabbath and the place of the law in Christian life in different ways. This page says only what the text says.

pages.title: The Ten Lepers
also: one in ten says thank you
pages.summary: On his way to Jerusalem Jesus passes between Samaria and Galilee. As he enters a village, ten men with leprosy stand at a distance and call out, asking Jesus, their Master, to have pity on them. He tells them to go and show themselves to the priests, and as they go, they are cleansed. One of them, seeing that he is healed, turns back, praising God in a loud voice, and falls at Jesus' feet to thank him. He is a Samaritan. Jesus asks whether ten were not cleansed, and where the other nine are, and why no one but this foreigner has come back to give thanks to God. Then he tells the man to get up and go, for his faith has made him well.
pages.look_closer: All ten obey and are cleansed on the way (verse 14), but only one comes back, and he is the outsider, a Samaritan (verse 16). Jesus' question is not angry: it points to missing thanks (verses 17-18).
lessons: Mercy is asked for, and Jesus hears it. The lepers call from a distance, and he answers (Luke 17:13-14).
Healing can come as we obey, step by step. They are cleansed as they go (Luke 17:14).
Gratitude is rare and precious. Only one in ten returns to thank him (Luke 17:15-18).
Thanks gives praise to God and meets Jesus. The Samaritan falls at his feet and hears that he has been made well (Luke 17:15-19).

pages.title: The Ten Plagues of Egypt
pages.summary: Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh to let God's people go, but Pharaoh's heart stays hard, and God sends ten plagues on Egypt. First the Nile turns to blood and the fish die. Then come frogs, gnats, flies, a deadly disease on the livestock, boils, hail, locusts and a thick darkness over the land. In several of them Egypt's magicians can only copy the sign or fail, and the land of Goshen, where the Israelites live, is spared. Several times Pharaoh promises to let the people go, and each time he changes his mind when the plague stops. Before the last plague the LORD tells Moses that one more will come, and that Pharaoh will then drive the Israelites out. Moses announces that at midnight every firstborn in Egypt will die, from the king's son to the servant's, but that not even a dog will growl at the Israelites.
pages.look_closer: The plagues touch the Nile, animals, crops and sun: things Egypt depended on. Exodus says they happen so that Egypt and Israel will know that he is the LORD (7:5; 10:2).
lessons: A hard heart can resist even clear signs. Pharaoh keeps changing his mind (Exodus 8:15; 9:34-35).
God protects his people in the middle of judgment. Goshen is spared (Exodus 8:22-23; 9:26).
God's power is greater than any false power. The magicians cannot match him (Exodus 8:18-19).
The tenth plague leads to the Passover, where God provides a way of rescue (Exodus 11:4-7; 12:12-13).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand how God hardened Pharaoh's heart, and how that relates to Pharaoh's own choices, in different ways. This page says only what the text says: the text says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that the LORD hardened it.

pages.title: The Tower of Babel
pages.summary: At one time the whole earth has one language and the same words. As people move eastward they find a flat valley in Shinar and settle there. They decide to make bricks and bake them hard, using brick for stone and tar for mortar. Then they say they will build a city and a tower reaching to the sky, to make a name for themselves, so that they will not be scattered over the whole earth. The LORD comes down to look at what they are building, and he says that one people with one language can do anything they plan, so he will confuse their language so that they cannot understand one another. The LORD scatters them over the whole earth, and they stop building the city. The place is called Babel, because that is where the LORD mixed up everyone's language.
pages.look_closer: The people want to make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered (verse 4). God scatters them anyway (verse 8). Later, at Pentecost, people from many languages hear one message in their own tongue (Acts 2:5-11).
lessons: Pride says, let us make a name for ourselves. God's plan is bigger than any human monument (Genesis 11:4).
Working together is powerful, for good or harm. God limits what united pride can do (Genesis 11:6-7).
God comes down to see. The great tower is small from his side (Genesis 11:5).
Babel's scattering looks forward to a day when all nations hear God's message together (Genesis 11:8-9; Acts 2:5-11).

pages.title: Spies Sent into Canaan
pages.summary: At the LORD's command Moses sends out twelve men, one leader from each tribe, to explore the land of Canaan. They spend forty days exploring and return carrying a huge cluster of grapes, with pomegranates and figs, from the Valley of Eshcol. They report that the land flows with milk and honey, but that the people are strong and the cities large and fortified. Caleb quiets the people and says they should go up and take the land, but the others spread a bad report, saying they felt like grasshoppers beside the giants. That night the whole community weeps and wishes it had died in Egypt, and some talk of choosing a leader and going back. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead with them not to rebel, because the LORD is with them. Because the people refuse to trust him, God says that the generation that grumbled will not enter the land, except Caleb and Joshua, and they will wander forty years.
pages.look_closer: Ten of the twelve see the same land and the same people, but they measure themselves against the giants instead of against God (13:31-33). Joshua and Caleb measure the giants against God (14:8-9). What we see depends on what we look at.
lessons: Facts can be true and still lead us wrong. The spies' report was accurate about the cities and the giants, but it left out the LORD (Numbers 13:28-33).
Fear spreads quickly, and so does faith. Caleb stands up and says they can do it (Numbers 13:30; 14:6-9).
Refusing to trust God has a cost. That generation does not enter the land (Numbers 14:22-23, 29-30).
God honors those who follow him wholeheartedly. Caleb and Joshua are spared (Numbers 14:24, 30).

pages.title: The Valley of Dry Bones
pages.summary: The hand of the LORD brings Ezekiel by the Spirit to a valley full of very dry bones. The LORD asks him whether these bones can live, and Ezekiel answers that only the Lord GOD knows. He is told to prophesy to the bones: they will hear the word of the LORD, and he will make breath enter them so that they live. As Ezekiel prophesies, there is a rattling sound and the bones come together, bone to bone, with tendons, flesh and skin covering them, but there is no breath in them. Then he is told to prophesy to the breath, and it enters them, and they come alive and stand up, a great army. The LORD explains that the bones stand for all of Israel's people, who say their bones are dried up and their hope is gone. He promises to open their graves, bring them up, place his Spirit within them so that they live, and return them to their own land.
pages.look_closer: The words for breath, wind and spirit are the same word in Hebrew, and Ezekiel plays on it: the wind, the breath and the Spirit of the LORD (verses 5-6, 9-10, 14). The bones live first by the word, and then by the breath.
lessons: God can bring life where hope is gone. The people say their bones are dried up (Ezekiel 37:11).
God's word does the work. As Ezekiel prophesies, the bones come together (Ezekiel 37:7-8).
The Spirit gives life. Breath enters them, and they stand up (Ezekiel 37:9-10, 14).
God keeps his promise to restore his people and open their graves (Ezekiel 37:12-14).
pages.doctrine_note: Christians understand this vision, including how it relates to the restoration of Israel and to the resurrection of the dead, in different ways. This page says only what the text says.

pages.title: The Visit of the Wise Men
pages.summary: After Jesus is born in Bethlehem, during the reign of King Herod, Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking where the child born king of the Jews is. They saw his star rising in the east and have traveled to worship him. Herod is disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him. He gathers the chief priests and scribes, who tell him from the prophet that a ruler will come from Bethlehem. Herod secretly finds out from the Magi when the star appeared and sends them to Bethlehem, asking them to report back so that he too can worship the child. The star goes ahead of them until it stops over the place where the child is. They are overjoyed, and in the house they see the child with Mary his mother, fall down and worship, and offer gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they return home by another road.
pages.look_closer: The Bible does not say there were three Magi; the three gifts are why people often say so. Notice also who is disturbed: the king in Jerusalem, and the whole city with him, while foreigners come to worship (verses 3, 11).
lessons: God draws people from far away to Jesus. These foreigners follow a star, while Israel's own leaders stay at home (Matthew 2:1-6, 9).
Real seeking ends in worship. The Magi fall down and give their best gifts (Matthew 2:10-11).
Not everyone is glad. Herod pretends he wants to worship, but he is planning harm, and fear of losing power has blinded him (Matthew 2:3, 7-8).
God protects the child. A dream warns the Magi, and they go home another way (Matthew 2:12).

pages.title: The Widow's Offering
pages.summary: Jesus sits down opposite the temple treasury and watches the crowd putting money into the offering box. Many rich people throw in large amounts. Then a poor widow comes and puts in two small copper coins, worth only a fraction of a penny. Jesus calls his disciples to him and says that this poor widow has given more than anyone else. They gave from their extra, but she, from her need, has given everything she had to live on.
pages.look_closer: Jesus is not looking at the amount but at what is left (verses 43-44). The rich gave from what they had extra; the widow gave all she had. The disciples had to be called over to see it (verse 43).
lessons: God measures a gift by the giver's heart and cost, not by its size (Mark 12:43-44).
The one who seems to give little may give the most. Jesus sees what no one else notices (Mark 12:41-44).
Generosity trusts God to care for the giver. She gives even her living (Mark 12:44).
